specAnchors.text: know the definition of the term 'half-life' and understand that it is different for different radioactive isotopes
use the concept of the half-life to carry out simple calculations on activity, including graphical methods

primer.text: No clock can time a single nucleus, but a sample keeps a timetable: the half-life. It is the time for the activity — or the nuclei count — to halve, it is fixed for each isotope, and it spans from fractions of a second to billions of years. Graphs turn it into easy arithmetic.

modules.title: Defining half-life
modules.opening: Half-life is the time needed for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample — equivalently the activity — to fall to half its starting value. Each isotope has its own fixed half-life, and measuring one is simply timing the fall from an initial activity to half of it.
keyPoints: Half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei to halve.
Equivalently, it is the time for the activity to fall to half its initial value.
Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years.
Measure the initial activity, then time the fall to half of that value.

low.restatement: Watch the meter: 800, 400, 200, 100… the gaps between halvings are all the same length — that gap is the half-life.
low.analogy: Half-life is like a queue leaving a stadium at a steady pattern — every ten minutes, half of whoever remains walks out.
low.examPointer: Both phrasings score: "number of nuclei halves" or "activity halves". Tie them together for full credit.

medium.restatement: Because decay probability per nucleus is constant, any fixed fraction of the remaining nuclei decays per unit time; the half is just the most convenient fraction, and halving repeats indefinitely — never quite reaching zero. Isotope identity fixes the probability, hence the half-life.
medium.analogy: A photocopier set to 50%: each copy is half the previous one, forever approaching but never hitting blank.
medium.examPointer: Half-life never "runs out" — after n half-lives, (1/2)ⁿ remains. Quote the table 100-50-25-12.5-6.25%.

modules.title: Half-life calculations
sourceHeadings: A graph can be used to make half-life calculations
modules.opening: Half-life arithmetic runs on repeated halving: divide the activity by 2 per half-life, or count halvings between two activities and divide the elapsed time by that count. On a graph, read the initial activity, find half of it, and read off the time — constant per isotope.
keyPoints: Each half-life halves the remaining activity or nuclei count.
Number of half-lives = elapsed time ÷ half-life.
On an activity-time graph, the half-life is the time to fall from any value to half of it.
The half-life read between 100%→50% equals that from 50%→25%.
A sample falling 880 → 440 → 220 Bq in one year has a half-life of 6 months.

low.restatement: Start 880 Bq: after one half-life 440, after two 220. Two halvings took a year, so one half-life is six months.
low.analogy: Keep halving a pizza: every cut takes the same time, and counting cuts tells you the kitchen’s rhythm.
low.examPointer: Write the halving chain explicitly (880 → 440 → 220) — the visible chain is the working examiners reward.

medium.restatement: Graphically, choose a clean starting value A₀, locate A₀/2 on the axis, and read the horizontal gap; the same gap recurs for A₀/2→A₀/4, which is the consistency check. Arithmetic-wise, converting elapsed time into half-life counts (n = t/T½) and applying (1/2)ⁿ to the initial activity solves both directions.
medium.analogy: Reading a half-life graph is like using a repeated staircase: every riser is the same height (the half) and the same tread (the half-life).
medium.examPointer: Technetium-style graph questions: draw the horizontal lines at A₀ and A₀/2 on the printed figure — visible construction earns method marks.

glossary.definition: The time for the number of unstable nuclei, or the activity, of a sample to halve.
The activity of a sample at the start of the measurement (A₀).
Finding the half-life by reading the time for the curve to fall from A₀ to A₀/2.

workedExample.prompt: The activity of a radioactive sample is 880 Bq. After one year it has dropped to 220 Bq. What is the half-life of this material?
steps: Two half-lives elapsed in one year.
